articles.title: US retail sales are surging. The Fed may make that harder to sustain
articles.summary: The Fed’s first rate rise since 2023 comes as US retail sales surge, putting consumer resilience – and retailers’ ability to turn it into profitable growth –...
articles.body:
The Fed's first rate rise since 2023 comes as US retail sales surge, creating a new test for consumer demand – and retailers' ability to turn resilient spending into profitable growth.

But for retailers, the Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023 means the question is no longer simply whether shoppers will keep buying.

It is whether retailers can maintain strong sales while the cost of borrowing, inventory and imported goods continues to rise.

The Fed raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points on Wednesday to 3.75%-4%. The median projection among Fed policymakers puts the rate at 4.1% at the end of both 2026 and 2027, up from 3.8% and 3.6%, respectively, in June.

Those projections are not commitments. But they raise the prospect of borrowing costs remaining relatively high for longer than previously expected.

The decision came just hours after new data showed US retail and food service sales jumping 1.2% in August to $773.9bn, the strongest monthly increase since March and comfortably above economists' expectations.

Sales were 6% higher than a year earlier, while July's decline was revised to 0.5%. The figures are adjusted for seasonal variation but not for price changes, meaning inflation accounts for part of the increase.

Even so, underlying demand remained strong. Retail sales excluding automobiles, petrol, building materials and food services rose 1.4% in August, their strongest increase since September 2024.

For retailers, that creates an unusual combination.

Demand is holding up. But that resilience also reduces the immediate pressure on the Fed to ease monetary policy as it tries to bring inflation back towards its 2% target.

The result could be a retail environment in which revenue remains resilient while the cost of generating that revenue increases.

August's rebound followed a weaker July, but other data suggest the underlying resilience in consumer spending has been more persistent.

The CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor recorded a tenth consecutive month of year-on-year sales growth in July.

Sales excluding automobile dealers and petrol stations increased 5.15% year on year, while core sales, which also exclude restaurants, rose 4.72%.

The Retail Monitor is based on anonymised credit and debit card transactions compiled by Affinity Solutions, providing a different measure from the Census Bureau's survey-based figures.

But the data also highlight an important distinction: consumers can keep spending while becoming increasingly price conscious.

articles.title: SEC unveils exemption for tokenized stock trading
articles.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) unveiled its long-awaited “innovation exemption” Thursday, a new order aimed at clearing the way for tokenized stock trading in the U.S. The order creates a pair of five-year exemptions. The first exempts platforms that host tokenized stock trading from the commission’s definition of an exchange, while the second exempts…
articles.body:
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) unveiled its long-awaited “innovation exemption” Thursday, a new order aimed at clearing the way for tokenized stock trading in the U.S.

The order creates a pair of five-year exemptions. The first exempts platforms that host tokenized stock trading from the commission’s definition of an exchange, while the second exempts liquidity providers in the space from its definition of a dealer.

“Over the past several years, advancements in distributed ledger technology have facilitated innovations in trading across non-security crypto assets,” the SEC noted in a fact sheet.

However, it suggested that tokenized stock trading platforms “may face substantial challenges with complying with the Federal securities laws without potentially burdensome changes to its business model.”

Tokenized stocks are digital versions of real-world stocks. They are represented by digital tokens on the blockchain, the technology that forms the foundation of cryptocurrency.

The SEC’s innovation exemption specifically applies to platforms that rely on automated market makers, which are often used by decentralized crypto exchanges.

Traditional market makers are separate financial institutions or individuals that provide liquidity for a market. Automated market makers, by contrast, depend on liquidity pools supplied by users and rely on an algorithm to automatically set prices.

To fall under the SEC’s exemption, these platforms have to be permissioned. Permissioned blockchains require some standards for people to access and trade on them, unlike public blockchains that are open to anyone.

Holders of the tokenized stock must also have the “same rights and privileges” as a traditional stock of an “equivalent class,” the SEC noted.

The new order comes just two days after the Clarity Act came up short in the Senate. The crypto regulation bill failed to secure enough support to clear a procedural hurdle on the Senate floor.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins hinted at the agency’s plans Wednesday.

“I have been unequivocal: with or without legislation, we will act decisively within the SEC’s statutory authority to deliver certainty for American investors and for the entrepreneurs shaping our technological future,” he wrote on the social platform X. “Stay tuned.”

articles.title: Trump administration allows truck drivers hauling gas, diesel to work longer hours
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Wednesday the Trump administration will temporarily increase how long gas and diesel truck drivers can drive, as fuel costs remain elevated amid the Iran war. Under the 90-day waiver from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), truck drivers hauling gasoline and diesel can drive for up to 16 hours…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Wednesday the Trump administration will temporarily increase how long gas and diesel truck drivers can drive, as fuel costs remain elevated amid the Iran war .

Under the 90-day waiver from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), truck drivers hauling gasoline and diesel can drive for up to 16 hours within a 24-hour window — an increase from the 14-hour limit under normal conditions. The waiver took effect Wednesday and expires on Dec. 16.

Drivers must still take a minimum of one six-hour break in their truck’s sleeper berth during the 24-hour period. If their vehicle does not have a separate bed area, the driver must take at least an eight-hour break during the aforementioned window.

The waiver applies to truck drivers “in good standing” and excludes “anyone with a conditional safety rating or an active out-of-service order,” the Transportation Department noted in a release .

“From unleashing American energy production to alleviating short-term supply chain pressures, the Trump Administration is constantly taking action to lower fuel prices,” Duffy wrote. “Our great American truckers will continue to haul the products that power America and keep our economy moving.”

The FMCSA waiver requires motor carriers to provide drivers with at least 10 consecutive hours of rest if they need it immediately. Motor carriers must also notify the agency within two business days of a crash.

Gas prices remain at more than $4 per gallon on average, as the war in Iran approaches the seven-month mark. The Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have hamstrung the global oil trade , with prices in the U.S. impacted despite it being a net exporter of oil .

The national average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.44 as of Thursday, up from roughly $4.28 a week ago and $1.50 higher than two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war, according to data from AAA .

Diesel in the U.S. also costs roughly $6.40 per gallon as of Thursday, with Californians seeing a price of about $8.35 per gallon on average, AAA reported.

President Trump on Wednesday reiterated his view that higher gas prices are worth enduring to ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done, remember that,” Trump said in North Carolina while stumping for GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley.

The president also predicted fuel prices will “come tumbling down” once the conflict ends, which he said last week will occur after November’s midterms .

articles.title: Kaepernick: Van Jones tried to broker a meeting between Trump, former QB
articles.summary: Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick revealed Wednesday that CNN analyst and former Obama administration adviser Van Jones attempted to broker a meeting between the football player and President Trump. Appearing on a MediasTouch podcast, host Ben Meiselas asked Kaepernick about a “Black Summit” the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback was invited to during Trump’s first…
articles.body:
Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick revealed Wednesday that CNN analyst and former Obama administration adviser Van Jones attempted to broker a meeting between the football player and President Trump.

Appearing on a MediasTouch podcast , host Ben Meiselas asked Kaepernick about a “Black Summit” the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback was invited to during Trump’s first term.

“What I’ve learned over the years is there is going to be a constant attempt to be able to co-opt people who are trying to work for the benefit of the people, and what we saw in this moment was, you know, part of that conversation,” Kaepernick said about the event. “What was relayed to me was the outreach came from Van Jones for this.”

“I don’t know the details around it because, candidly, as soon as it came up as, ‘Hey, here is the opportunity,’ it was immediately rejected,” he continued.

The president’s relationship with Kaepernick throughout his first term was complicated as Trump criticized the quarterback for kneeling on the field during the national anthem in protest of racial injustice.

“But I will tell you — you cannot disrespect our country, our flag, our anthem, you cannot do that,” Trump said at the time.

Trump also stated he would support the NFL suspending Kaepernick indefinitely because of his protest.

Kaepernick said Trump’s actions made him think the invite to the summit was “a facade that he’s working for Black people or trying to be in the benefit of Black people,” but “history shows otherwise.”

“This is after him going out publicly and trying to target me in my employment,” he added.

Kaepernick specifically called out connections between Trump and the Reform Alliance — where Jones formerly served as CEO — saying, “Ultimately, what we see is on the other side of that, you know, pardons being handed out, and we’re seeing those pay-for-play right now.”

Kaepernick has been out of the NFL since March 2017, when he opted out of his 49ers contract, though he has not officially retired. He filed a grievance at the time that accused NFL owners of colluding to keep him from playing.

The lawsuit named Trump and former Vice President Mike Pence as a “colluding force” to prevent him from signing a contract within the league. The case was reportedly settled in 2019 for less than $10 million.

In the same year, Trump said he would “love” to see Kaepernick back in the league, noting that NFL owners would sign him “if he was good enough.”

articles.title: Oral pill could provide new option for people with sleep apnea
articles.summary: Around 30 million people in the U.S. suffer from the disease, according to the American Lung Association, but millions go undiagnosed.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — An oral drug designed to treat sleep apnea showed promising results in a recent clinical trial, suggesting there may be another alternative on the market soon for people who don’t like using Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machines.

In the phase 3 trial, 646 adults with mild to severe obstructive sleep apnea were given the once-nightly pill AD109, Science Daily reported , based on materials provided by the American Thoracic Society. Researchers found that more than 40 percent of participants’ conditions improved to a less severe OSA classification, while 18 percent achieved complete control of the disease.

The trial also found that the number of breathing interruptions fell by 44 percent in patients who took the medication, while the placebo group only showed a less than 20 percent reduction, according to Science Daily. The outlet said AD109 is intended to work by supporting throat muscles, “so the airway is less likely to sag or collapse during sleep.”

Obstructive sleep apnea is a breathing disorder that occurs when the throat muscles relax and repeatedly block the airway during sleep. It affects nearly one billion adults worldwide and is linked to serious health problems, including heart disease and stroke.

Around 30 million people in the U.S. suffer from the disease, according to the American Lung Association , but millions go undiagnosed and untreated.

For those who are diagnosed, CPAP machines are the most common treatment ; however, some people cannot tolerate them or decline to use them. The participants in the study, which was published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, all fit into one of those categories, per Science Daily.

It is important to note that while side effects were described as “mild and expected,” 21 percent of patients in the study stopped taking the drug because of them, the outlet added. Still, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has given AD109 the Fast Track designation, “reflecting the need for effective and well-tolerated drug therapies for the condition.”

NewsNation recently reported on a review published in JAMA Otolaryngology that found GLP-1 drugs may reduce the severity of obesity-related sleep apnea.

NewsNation staff contributed to this report.

articles.summary: Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) on Thursday introduced legislation to phase out waiting periods for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Medicare benefits. Kim’s bill, the Stop the Wait Act, would phase out the five-month waiting period for SSDI benefits over five years as well as eliminate the 24-month waiting period for Medicare disability benefits. The…
articles.body:
Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) on Thursday introduced legislation to phase out waiting periods for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Medicare benefits.

Kim’s bill, the Stop the Wait Act, would phase out the five-month waiting period for SSDI benefits over five years as well as eliminate the 24-month waiting period for Medicare disability benefits.

The senator from New Jersey cited data from the Government Accountability Office that found more than 100,000 people died between fiscal 2008 and 2019 while waiting for a final decision on their SSDI benefits. This figure represents roughly 1.2 percent of total disability applicants who filed an appeal.

“It is horrifying that any American should be forced to endure months or even years of waiting for benefits they worked hard to earn. Care cannot be put on hold. Congress needs to step up for our disability community and end these harmful waiting periods once and for all,” Kim said in a statement.

A similar bill with the same title was introduced last February by Democratic Rep. Lloyd Doggett (Texas), but it did not progress after being referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.

SSDI benefits are paid to people who are unable to work because of a medical condition that is expected to last at least on year or potentially result in death. Diseases of the musculoskeletal system and connective tissue are by far the most common conditions reported among SSDI beneficiaries, accounting for roughly 65 percent, according to a 2024 report from the Social Security Administration.

In a statement, Kim’s office argued that Congress had already moved to eliminate waiting periods for certain situations, such as for people with ALS.

The bill has been endorsed by the Federation of American Hospitals, American Association of People with Disabilities, the Alzheimer’s Association, Pandemic Patients and the National Alliance on Mental Illness, among others.

articles.title: Your robotaxi might be a narc
articles.summary: Waymo called the cops on two passengers after detecting a gun in the vehicle. The incident raises questions about the limits of privacy inside an autonomous vehicle.
articles.body: In early September, two teenagers got into a Waymo, but then ended up in the back of a police car. The robotaxi company said it detected “a violation of our terms of service involving a firearm,” pulled the car over, and alerted emergency services, according to the Los Angeles Times. Police arrested the passengers after allegedly finding a loaded AR-style “ghost gun” in the vehicle. The arrests exposed a lot of unanswered questions about privacy and autonomous vehicles, including what they are recording, what they do with the footage, and how much privacy riders should expect while riding inside them. Waymo’s camera-covered cars have already been drawn into the debate over privacy and surveillance. On a number of occasions, law enforcement agencies have obtained search warrants for footage captured by its cars, according to Bloomberg. Last year, the LAPD obtained footage of a hit-and-run that was recorded by a nearby Waymo vehicle. During anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles, five Waymos were vandalized and set on fire amid questions about whether the vehicles could be capturing images of protesters that might be used as evidence to identify or arrest them. Waymo does not publicly disclose how many law enforcement requests it receives or how often it complies. Those concerns echo the backlash against Flock’s network of automated license-plate readers, which have given police the ability to track cars across jurisdictions and have prompted growing fears about government surveillance and misuse. Unlike fixed Flock cameras, Waymos move through cities carrying cameras both outside and inside their vehicles. [Image: Waymo Ojai autonomous robotaxi travels through the Fourth and Howard streets intersection outside Moscone West, which displays banners for the 2026 Pokemon World Championships, San Francisco, California, August 20, 2026. The latest case of the arrested teens takes those concerns a step further. Police did not approach Waymo after a crime looking for footage its cameras happened to capture. Waymo detected something inside the car and initiated the police response itself. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina told The Verge in an email that the company uses its internal cameras to help enforce its terms of service, including detecting prohibited items and behavior. She said it uses automated technology to help Waymo’s teams identify potential violations, such as the presence of firearms inside the vehicle. “If Waymo detects a firearm in the vehicle, we may reach out to local law enforcement,” she added. Waymo did not explain how its automated system determines whether something may be a firearm, how confident it has to be before something gets flagged, what role humans play between an automated alert and a call to police, or what other violations of its terms of service might prompt a police response. Those are important omissions. This wasn’t a human taxi driver deciding to call 911. It was a driverless car, equipped with cameras and an AI brain, escalating a situation involving its passengers to police. Bob Somers, a former engineer at autonomous vehicle company Zoox and technical adviser to the AV-safety nonprofit SAVE-US, said he would expect Waymo’s system to look for a range of potentially dangerous weapons and behaviors. The software may not need to decide with certainty that it has seen a firearm. It could instead flag something that resembles one for further review, he said. “If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on,” Somers said. Phil Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University professor emeritus who researches autonomous vehicle safety, said computer vision systems can be trained to recognize objects and potentially dangerous situations. "“If there is a certain set of objects detected, then that would probably loop in a remote operator to take a look at what’s going on.”" - Bob Somers “If you can train a computer to look at the road and decide how to drive, you can train a computer to decide if somebody’s holding a gun,” Koopman said. But, he added, those systems are “never 100 percent accurate.” That’s where the unanswered question about human review becomes important. A human taxi driver who sees a passenger holding something has context. They’ve been in the car for the entire ride. They can hear what the passengers are saying and ask questions. They can decide whether the object is a real gun, a toy, or something else entirely. Back in July, Waymo reported two teens to the police for underage drinking and shooting a toy gun loaded with water beads from the vehicle. It was not clear whether the teens ultimately faced any charges. A remote worker brought in to review a flagged moment might not have all of that context because they haven’t experienced the entire ride the way a human driver would. Waymo says its interior microphones are generally active only during calls with Rider Support or when riders enable them, meaning a reviewer may not be able to hear what preceded the flagged moment. As of earlier this year, Waymo has about 70 “remote assistance agents” on duty at a given time in the US and the Philippines, who “provide advice and support to the Waymo Driver but do not directly control, steer, or drive the vehicle.” Waymo has not said whether the people reviewing possible violations inside its cars are among those agents. “It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous,” Koopman said. Beyond undermining riders’ trust in robotaxis, a false alarm could put passengers at risk during a police encounter. Then there’s the question of what Waymo tells riders to expect. Without a driver in the front seat, robotaxis can feel more private than they actually are. In 2023, the San Francisco Standard spoke with four people who said they had hooked up or had sex in Cruise robotaxis, despite the cameras inside them. The publication could not find anyone who said they had done so in a Waymo, but the episodes illustrate how readily passengers can mistake the absence of a human driver for the absence of a witness. Waymo’s terms of service requires riders to comply with applicable laws and prohibits them from creating a dangerous condition, carrying weapons “or anything that resembles a weapon, e.g. toy gun,” or using drugs. Riders must be at least 18 to ride alone in San Francisco. The two riders arrested this month allegedly violated both the age and weapons restrictions. The terms say Waymo can suspend or terminate a rider’s access if it believes the rider has violated the rules. Earlier this year, Waymo suspended the account used to book a ride after three boys were photographed hanging out the windows of the vehicle and taking selfies. But they do not plainly tell passengers that the company may call the police based on what it sees inside the car. "“It’s really important that Waymo gets it right when they alert the police to something dangerous.”" - Phil Koopman Waymo’s public camera policy says its interior cameras can be used to “check that in-car rules are being followed” and “promote safety and security.” It says Waymo Support may review recorded video after an issue is brought to the company’s attention and, in urgent circumstances, access live video during a trip. The policy also says Waymo may share certain data with law enforcement as needed to comply with legal requirements, enforce agreements, or protect the safety of riders and others. But it doesn’t specify that automated monitoring inside the vehicle may trigger Waymo itself to contact police. Hayley Tsukayama, director of state affairs at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, called Waymo’s public policies “very broad.” Riders shouldn’t have to infer from language about “safety and security” that their behavior could result in a police response, she said, adding that Waymo should clearly disclose that possibility before passengers get into the car. “I’m not condoning illegal behavior in rideshares,” she said, but “if they’re going to share it with authorities, then that should be clearly stated in the policy.” As it stands, Tsukayama said, “it is outside of the expectations of consumers.” Then again, robotaxis themselves are outside the norm. As they become more common, riders may have to develop a new set of expectations about what happens inside them. A human driver can decide how to respond to what happens in their car. In a robotaxi, cameras and software can flag what happens inside, remote workers may become involved, and the vehicle can pull over while police are summoned. Waymo’s system may have helped police recover an illegal firearm in this case. But the incident also raises a more basic question about what kind of space a robotaxi is: a ride with cameras for safety, a continuously monitored space, or a system that can call the cops on its own passengers. That question is already showing up in fiction. Robotaxis are making their debut as villains in Road Rage, an upcoming short film about a driverless car that turns against humans. One of the film’s more unsettling ideas is that a robotaxi could end up acting less like transportation and more like law enforcement. This month offered a glimpse of what that might look like.

articles.title: Judge orders Google to change ad auction rules
articles.summary: A federal judge has ordered Google to change its rules for auctioning online advertising on its platforms after finding last year that the search giant had an illegal monopoly over the technology connecting publishers and advertisers. The remedies were made public late Wednesday, when U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema unsealed her opinion from earlier this…
articles.body:
A federal judge has ordered Google to change its rules for auctioning online advertising on its platforms after finding last year that the search giant had an illegal monopoly over the technology connecting publishers and advertisers.

The remedies were made public late Wednesday, when U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema unsealed her opinion from earlier this month.

In the decision, Brinkema ruled that Google did not have to break up its ad tech business, rejecting the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) request to force the company to sell off its advertising exchange or open-source the technology behind its platform for publishers.

She accepted “most” of the behavioral remedies put forward by Google and the federal government, but the specifics remained under seal until Wednesday.

“The Court finds that structural remedies are neither realistic nor needed and that the parties’ substantially overlapping behavioral remedies as modified in this Memorandum Opinion will be sufficient to ‘effectively pry open to competition’ the ad tech markets,” Brinkema wrote in the opinion.

The judge suggested the DOJ’s rationale for a breakup “boils down to a lack of trust that Google will comply with an Order from this Court and an unrealistic desire for certainty.”

“Lack of trust alone or desire for ‘guaranteed certainty’ cannot justify divestiture,” she added.

However, Google will be barred from engaging in the behavior that ultimately prompted Brinkema to rule last April that it had improperly secured monopoly power over two markets involved in selling online ads.

Under the decision, the company will not be allowed to enforce policies tying its publisher-side platform, DoubleClick for Publishers (DFP), to its ad exchange platform, AdX.

The opinion also bars Google from reimplementing a series of functions that required publishers using DFP to give AdX special treatment on bids for ad space.

The firm is required to make both platforms interoperable with header bidding software, which allows publishers to offer up ad space to multiple ad exchanges before moving forward.

It also must make AdX interoperable with rival publisher-side platforms and provide publishers with data from both AdX and DFP.

Both platforms are barred from prioritizing Google’s own products, as is the company’s advertiser-side platform, AdWords.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward touted the ruling as “a significant victory for this Department’s efforts to protect and restore competition.”

“We will continue to review the opinion to consider the Department’s options,” he added in a statement. “Under President Trump’s and Attorney General Blanche’s leadership, we will never cease fighting for fair competition.”

It marks the second time that a judge has declined to break up Google’s products.

While U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ruled in August 2024 that the company had an illegal monopoly over online search, he ultimately rejected the DOJ’s request to force Google to sell off its Chrome browser last September.

articles.title: Environment, health groups sue over Trump move to wipe out climate rules for power plants
articles.summary: Environmental and public health-focused organizations are suing the Trump administration over its move to wipe out most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants. The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the suit on Thursday. The move comes…
articles.body:
Environmental and public health-focused organizations are suing the Trump administration over its move to wipe out most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the suit on Thursday.

The move comes just days after the administration finalized its move to gut the nation’s climate rules for coal and gas plants, eliminating the vast majority of rules that the Biden administration said would prevent 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon emissions through 2047, the equivalent of taking 328 million gas-powered cars off the road for a year.

That’s because existing coal and new gas plants will no longer have to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

As the electric sector makes up a quarter of the U.S.’s total planet-heating emissions, that move could be one of the Trump administration’s most consequential climate rollbacks.

The administration estimated that it could save $310 billion.

The groups that sued Thursday said the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has a legal responsibility to limit planet-warming emissions, and that not doing so would have significant health consequences.

“Repealing these standards without a replacement is an abdication of EPA’s legal responsibility to protect public health and the environment,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at NRDC, in a written statement. “The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation. The EPA’s legal reasoning is fatally flawed, so we are going to court.”

“Emissions from power plants drive climate change, and climate change is a health emergency,” said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “Measures that clean up power plant emissions also clean up other lung-harming pollutants at the same time. EPA has the authority and the responsibility to protect people’s health from air pollution.”

The EPA declined The Hill’s request for comment on the lawsuit. When it put forward the rule, the agency said that its move was a money saver.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

articles.title: Trump administration reduces protections for endangered species again
articles.summary: The Trump administration has further reduced protections for endangered species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). That law prohibits any “take” of endangered species, which it defines as to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct.” The administration recently repealed a previous definition of…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has further reduced protections for endangered species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

That law prohibits any “take” of endangered species, which it defines as to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct.”

The administration recently repealed a previous definition of prohibited “harm” under the law, now saying that in implementing that regulation, it will only consider an action “taking” a species if it is intentional.

“The Harm Rule rescinded the Services’ regulatory definitions of ‘harm,’ and adopted Justice [Antonin] Scalia’s interpretation of ‘take’ set out in the dissent in Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon,” the memo states.

“Under Justice Scalia’s interpretation, ‘take’ reaches only an affirmative act that is intentionally and purposefully directed at a particular animal,” it said.

The administration says, for example, that a ship that “inadvertently” strikes a whale “has not taken it,” and that felling a tree is not a take of bats residing in it.

The internal Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) memo was obtained and made public by the Center for Biological Diversity on Thursday.

Brett Hartl, the group’s government affairs director, said “Fish and Wildlife is going to effectively, I think, be entirely muzzled by this memo.”

“They are basically going to be told … ‘Look the other way on virtually all types of harmed or endangered species. We are not in the business of enforcing that anymore,'” he told The Hill.

The Interior Department, which oversees FWS, said via email that that the memo “accurately reflects the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of ‘harm.'”

“Under the guidance, the ESA’s prohibition on ‘take’ continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife,” said an unsigned statement from the department.

The move is the latest of multiple bites the Trump administration has taken out of the ESA. In July, it rolled back protections for at-risk animals considered “threatened,” a step below endangered.

articles.title: Human rights experts: ‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe US committed war crimes with Iran strikes
articles.summary: The United Nations’s fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it found “reasonable grounds” that the U.S. military committed war crimes in two airstrikes inside Iran and accused Iran’s government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its citizens during the forceful crackdown on anti-government protests earlier this year. The mission is made up of independent…
articles.body:
The United Nations’s fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it found “reasonable grounds” that the U.S. military committed war crimes in two airstrikes inside Iran and accused Iran’s government of carrying out crimes against humanity against its citizens during the forceful crackdown on anti-government protests earlier this year.

The mission is made up of independent experts and was established in November 2022 by the U.N.’s top human rights body, the Human Rights Council.

The Pentagon told The Hill it declines to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization, adding that the department’s investigation “remains ongoing” and “we have nothing to announce at the moment.”

In late February, at the start of the U.S. war against Iran, an all-girls school in the south of the country, Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School, was struck, killing nearly 160 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren.

The U.N. experts concluded in their report that the strike was a Tomahawk missile fired by the U.S. military on Feb. 28 at the school in Minab.

“The Mission considered the area of operations of the parties; its assessment of the origin and type of weapon used; several corroborated reports indicating that a preliminary U.S. military inquiry found U.S. forces responsible for the strike; the U.S. CENTCOM Commander’s assertion that the strike on the school ‘correlates’ with a U.S. strike; and the fact that the U.S. is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles,” the group said in the 18-page report .

Top Trump administration officials have repeatedly said the U.S. military follows the laws of armed conflict and does not target civilians. Military officials have said for months that the Minab school strike is under investigation.

The mission also said a strike on a sports complex in Lamerd city, Fars Province, on Feb. 28, where more than 20 people were killed, was done by U.S. Central Command (Centcom) forces. Open-source analysis done by multiple news outlets found that the U.S.-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) was used in the airstrike.

Centcom said in March that U.S. forces did not fire missiles at Lamerd that day.

“The Mission notes key visual features of the PrSM’s silhouette identifiable in verified video, namely the long and sharp nose cone, smooth fuselage and short tail fins at the very base of the exhaust nozzle. It also observes that the missile detonations seen in verified videos occur directly above the target and not upon impact, which is consistent with a PrSM’s airburst’ mechanism,” the group said in the report.

The report also said Iran’s government carried out “violent repression” against anti-government protesters during late 2025 and early 2026 with widespread lethal forces that resulted in mass killings.

The killings by state security forces took place in all 31 provinces, with the highest death tolls reported in Karaj, Mashhad, Isfahan, Rasht and Tehran.

Security forces fired at protesters from rooftops. In Karaj, the regime forces fired tear gas to “trap demonstrators in narrow alleys before shooting them,” the report said, adding that at least 220 children were killed.

“Security forces also attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded protestors and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care,” the experts said.

The mission “has strong grounds to believe” that the true number of those killed and injured is “significantly higher” than Iran’s government figures of 3,038 people killed and about 25,000 injured, which were presented in February.

“Iran has also used the death penalty against children in connection with the 2025/2026 protests, meaning individuals under the age of 18 at the time of the alleged offence,” the experts said in the report. “This is absolutely prohibited under international human rights law.”

A scammer might buy that information, pull it from people-search sites or piece it together from public sources. That means hurricane charity scams can start before a storm even hits. By the time a hurricane dominates the news, a fraudster may already know who could respond to a donation pitch. One Justice Department case shows how dangerous that kind of targeting can become. Epsilon Data Management used transactional data and a database covering 100 million U.S. households to identify "responsive buyers." Prosecutors said two executives, Robert Reger and David Lytle, spent about a decade knowingly selling targeted lists to fraudsters. One client used those lists to defraud more than 218,000 people out of over $23.7 million. More than 12,000 victims got hit more than 20 times. A judge sentenced Reger to 10 years in prison and Lytle to four years. Epsilon also paid $150 million in penalties and victim compensation, with $122 million returned to more than 200,000 victims. The Epsilon prosecution focused on mass-mailing fraud rather than hurricane charity scams. Still, it shows how personal data and behavioral signals can help fraudsters choose targets before a pitch lands. Separate FBI data shows the cost of charity fraud. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded 662 charity complaints and $7,907,609 in reported losses in 2025. Why fake charity scams can reach almost anyone A scammer does not need a history of bad donations to target you. Fraudsters can reach people through purchased lists, public records, robocalls and other marketing channels. James Trankle ran three fake charities, including the "Disabled and Paralyzed Veterans Fund," the "National Breast Cancer Awareness Fund" and the "Children's Leukemia of America Fund." He mailed solicitations to thousands of people and collected more than 1,600 personal checks. Then he used donor banking information to create counterfeit checks. Many victims were older adults. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison. Travis Peterson ran a six-year scheme using millions of robocalls and other outreach to solicit donations for sham veterans' charities. Prosecutors said he often targeted senior citizens. A judge sentenced him to 41 months in prison and ordered him to pay $541,032.10 in restitution. MINNESOTA NONPROFIT ACCUSED OF SIPHONING $6.5M TO FUND VEGAS TRIPS, LUXURY CARS, PRIVATE LIQUOR STORE Why hurricane charity scams get worse after storms Natural disasters create urgency and confusion while bringing out people's desire to help. FEMA also warned residents to be alert for impostors posing as inspectors or disaster workers. The FTC has warned that scammers quickly exploit weather emergencies with fake charities and copycat organizations. Some imitate real charity names or create websites that appear tied to a disaster. Meanwhile, the Atlantic hurricane season runs through November 30, and NOAA identifies September 10 as the climatological peak. The key is slowing down long enough to verify who wants your money and taking a few steps to protect yourself before you donate. 1) Verify the charity independently Look it up on Charity Navigator, BBB Wise Giving Alliance at Give.org, CharityWatch or the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search. Avoid links in unexpected texts or emails. Instead, go directly to the charity's official website. 2) Be careful with payment methods The FTC warns that scammers may insist on cash, gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency. If you donate, a credit card or check gives you more protection and a clearer paper trail. 3) Slow down when someone pushes urgency A demand to donate immediately should make you stop and verify the organization before sending money. Legitimate charities will give you time to research them and decide whether you want to give. 4) Watch for copycat charity names and websites Scammers may use names that sound like established charities or web addresses that differ by only a few characters. Before donating, check the spelling of the charity's name and make sure you are on its official website. 5) Do not trust donation links in texts, emails or social media posts A donation request can look convincing even when it comes from a compromised account or impersonates a real charity. Do not assume a fundraiser is legitimate because a friend shared it. Go directly to the charity's official website instead of clicking the donation link and use strong antivirus software to help protect you from malicious links, phishing sites and malware that may be hiding behind fraudulent donation requests. 6) Check your statement after you donate Review your credit card or bank statement after making a donation. Confirm that you were charged only the amount you approved and check that you were not signed up for recurring donations you did not intend to make. articles.title: After months of vacancies, Kennedy revamps preventive services panel with new members
articles.summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday named eight new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), an influential panel of experts who determine what preventive medical services insurers must cover for free. For the first time, physician specialists, as opposed to only primary care doctors, will fill the specialized…
articles.body:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday named eight new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), an influential panel of experts who determine what preventive medical services insurers must cover for free.

For the first time, physician specialists, as opposed to only primary care doctors, will fill the specialized Health and Human Services (HHS) task force. Primary care doctors are generalists with experience across the broad range of topics the panel covers.

“We are strengthening the Task Force to ensure it asks hard questions, follows the evidence wherever it leads, and maintains the highest standards of scientific integrity,” Kennedy said in a statement announcing the new appointees.

In the past, the task force typically called in specialists to consult on discussions relevant to their expertise, but it did not traditionally welcome nonprimary care doctors to join the panel to avoid potential conflicts of interest tied to their medical specialty.

The new members include specialists in oncology, cardiology and gastroenterology. For example, its newly appointed chair, Seth Corey, is a pediatric hematologist-oncologist at Cleveland Clinic.

The panel also welcomed a finance professor who has expertise in health insurance, the value of healthcare services and related policy. Though he does not have a medical degree.

In a statement, the American Medical Association (AMA) said the panel must continue to prioritize primary care physicians.

“We believe maintaining a strong primary care voice must remain central to its work. As the USPSTF moves forward, its recommendations must continue to be based on a transparent, rigorous, independent scientific process and informed by the perspective of physicians who deliver preventive care to patients every day,” AMA President Willie Underwood III said.

The task force is an independent panel of experts that reviews evidence and makes recommendations for services such as cancer screenings, HIV prevention medications and more.

The panel makes its recommendations using a grading scale, and ObamaCare requires insurers to cover services the task force recommends with a “grade” of A or B at no cost to patients.

Kennedy has been highly critical of the panel, and his quest to overhaul it has raised alarms .

“That task force has been lackadaisical. It’s not been doing its job,” he told a House committee in April. “If it had been doing its job, we would have early screening for Alzheimer’s.”

During a separate hearing, Kennedy said the agency was “bringing new members on who have a clear mission,” though he did not elaborate on what it would entail.

Former members said the HHS has blocked the panel from beginning work on new topics and suppressed the release of four new guidelines, including updated recommendations on cervical cancer screenings.

Kennedy has prevented the panel from meeting for more than a year and left it with multiple vacancies after declining to replace members whose terms expired. In May, the HHS secretary fired the panel’s two top leaders .

The task force chair and vice chair would typically be involved in screening and vetting potential new members.

But without its leadership, Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Director Roger Klein — a political appointee — has been heading the task force’s efforts.

AcademyHealth, a nonprofit representing health policy researchers, said there are significant questions about how the new members were chosen.

“The public should be able to see how the new members were chosen and vetted. The Task Force has established procedures for disclosing and managing conflicts of interest. Those disclosures, and the process used to evaluate them, should be public,” the organization said in a statement.

Aside from concerns about new members, AcademyHealth noted that the task force relies on the scientific support of AHRQ. But the agency has lost a significant number of staff over the past year and canceled more than 150 research grants.

“Appointing new members doesn’t undo any of that. The best-qualified panel in the world still needs rigorous, current evidence to evaluate. Without it, there’s nothing to grade,” the organization said.

Kennedy has repeatedly accused the task force of poor performance.

articles.title: Almost 2 in 3 say AI development a bad thing: Survey
articles.summary: A poll released by Marquette University Law School on Thursday found that almost two-thirds of Americans say they think the development of AI is a bad thing. In the poll, 64 percent of respondents said AI is bad for society, and 36 percent said it’s a good thing, according to a release. This marked a…
articles.body:
A poll released by Marquette University Law School on Thursday found that almost two-thirds of Americans say they think the development of AI is a bad thing.

In the poll, 64 percent of respondents said AI is bad for society, and 36 percent said it’s a good thing, according to a release . This marked a 6-point drop from a July poll, in which 70 percent of people said they viewed AI as a bad thing. The number was at 65 percent in May and 70 percent in April.

But pollsters also found that even with the sour outlook on the technology, 69 percent of respondents said they use AI, compared with 31 percent who said they don’t. This is an increase from all three of Marquette’s previous polls.

Respondents saw few benefits to data centers, with 33 percent saying data centers “maintain U.S. leadership in AI. Thirty percent said the digital economy relies on data centers, 29 percent said data centers produce new permanent jobs and 19 percent said they provide construction jobs.

Among respondents, 54 percent told Marquette the top significant cost of data centers is the high water use, followed by 51 percent who said the centers drive up electricity costs.

A smaller number of respondents — 30 percent — mentioned how the centers replace rural or agricultural land. Fourteen percent said the tax subsidies are not worth it, while another 14 percent said the centers create few permanent jobs. Thirteen percent also noted the centers produce too much noise.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill and tech leaders have called for more guardrails to be set up to regulate AI. Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.) called for a one-month “ safety stand-down ” to allow independent experts to come together and talk about what “red lines” should be established and then have Congress work to put those red lines into law.

Calls for regulating AI have grown after a researcher at Anthropic warned last week that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

On the other side of the aisle, Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) blocked Sen. John Kennedy’s (R-La.) request to pass legislation that would require tech companies to develop a “kill switch” for AI if it posed a threat to humanity.

President Trump, a longtime critic of regulations in general, wrote on Truth Social on Monday that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

This reaction prompted Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who supports AI regulation, to say it was “embarrassing … how ignorant this president is about the dangers of AI.”

The Marquette University survey was conducted Sept. 2-9 and included 1,023 respondents with a margin of error of 4.3 percentage points.

articles.title: FAA sees $100 million cost from tariffs on US air traffic control modernization plan
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - The head of the U. Federal Aviation Administration said the agency expects about a $100 million cost from tariffs on ‌the gov...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - The head of the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration said the agency expects about a $100 million cost from tariffs on ‌the government's more than $12.5 billion air traffic control modernization plan.

U.S. Representative Rick ‌Larsen, a Washington Democrat who is ranking member of the committee overseeing the FAA, told Reuters that FAA Administrator ​Bryan Bedford informed lawmakers the $100 million tariff cost was largely due to air traffic radar systems they are purchasing. Larsen criticized the tariffs for increasing the government's costs.

"I've asked them for specific amounts and what equipment is being impacted," Larsen said. "I'm not a fan of ‌tariffs. We're trying to get ⁠the national aerospace system modernized and we're going to pay tariffs because of the president's policies."

Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding last year to ⁠address the aging air traffic control system and boost controller hiring following decades of complaints about airport congestion and flight delays, as well as a series of technology issues in recent ​years. The ​FAA wants at least another $10 billion for ​phase two.

The cost of telecommunications upgrades ‌has jumped from $4.75 billion to $5.91 billion, a government report said this week. Bedford said outdated telecom copper wires should be replaced by September 2027.

Bedford also said two radar suppliers, RTX's Collins Aerospace and Spain-based Indra Group, were moving radar production to U.S. facilities in Largo, Florida, and Kansas, respectively. He did not say where the production was moving from.

In January, the FAA awarded $780 ‌million in contracts to RTX and Indra to ​replace up to 612 ground-based radars, most of which ​date back to the 1980s. Bedford ​said earlier that many radars exceeded their intended service life and ‌are increasingly expensive to maintain and difficult ​to support.

In March, RTX ​said it was investing $26.5 million in its Largo facility to expand production, while Indra said it was investing $7.5 million in its radar facility in a Kansas ​City suburb to build next-generation ‌air traffic surveillance radars.

Indra is also building next-generation digital radios for the ​FAA at the Kansas site under a separate $244 million contract.

articles.body:
President Trump announced Thursday that the U.S. is making “major progress” in establishing its own Army base in Poland.

“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance,” the president said in a Truth Social post , which also praised the “bold” leadership of Polish President Karol Nawrocki.

The Pentagon referred The Hill to the White House for comment. The White House and the U.S. Embassy in Poland did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for further information on the base.

Earlier this month, top Polish government and military officials met in Poland with a U.S. delegation led by a Pentagon policy office leader, Will Cappelletti — its deputy assistant secretary of defense for Europe and NATO policy. The group discussed enhancing the U.S. military presence in the central European nation.

Polish ‌Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz met with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during a June visit to Brussels. The Polish official indicated then the country was open to having another U.S. military facility.

The Polish defense minister is set to meet with Hegseth again at the Pentagon, where the two are planning to discuss potential Russian threats on NATO’s eastern flank, central European country security and a proposed PAC-3 missile service center, according to Polish broadcaster Polsat News.

Earlier this year, the Pentagon paused the long-planned deployment of 4,000 service members to Poland, prompting deep frustration and concern from lawmakers in both parties who support a strong NATO alliance.

The announcement comes as the Pentagon is conducting a Europe posture review, overseen in consultations with NATO allies and Congress. The assessment is slated to be completed in December.

There are about 10,000 U.S. service members typically stationed in Poland on a rotational basis. But Trump announced in May that the U.S. would send 5,000 additional troops to the country.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) said in June after a closed-door meeting with Hegseth that the Defense secretary was “committed” to replacing the unit in Poland but hasn’t followed through.

In July, Bacon, a vocal backer of NATO, told The Hill that the Pentagon has not dispatched the Army brigade.

articles.title: US troops need to prepare for combat around the moon: Joint Chiefs chair
articles.summary: U.S. troops must prepare for combat around the moon in addition to Earth’s orbit, according to Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine. Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Wednesday, Caine said the U.S. military should make the necessary moves now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win ……
articles.body:
U.S. troops must prepare for combat around the moon in addition to Earth’s orbit, according to Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine.

Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Wednesday, Caine said the U.S. military should make the necessary moves now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space.”

Caine, President Trump’s top military adviser, spoke of fighting in space a few days after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed the U.S. launched a weapon into orbit to protect American troops.

Meink, speaking at the same conference Monday, did not elaborate on the type of weapon that is now in space or when it was launched, but he said it will “make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”

The Washington Post reported the weapon could allow America’s forces to take out an enemy’s satellite should it be used to target U.S. troops or a satellite.

Speaking to reporters separately, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, head of the force’s Combat Forces Command, said the Space Force is preparing for conflict outside the Earth’s atmosphere and around the moon because “humanity is advancing deeper into space,” The Associated Press reported.

“Our potential adversaries such as the PRC [People’s Republic of China] are actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space,” Gagnon said, noting that Washington is looking to double the size of the Space Force over the next five years to roughly 25,000 service members.

“We have capabilities in the military because we are preparing to defend the nation,” Gagnon said, according to the AP. “The reason we have the capabilities is to help create deterrence.”

articles.title: Senate Democrat blocks House-passed bill on data center electricity costs
articles.summary: Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) blocked Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Thursday effort to unanimously pass a bill that seeks to force states to consider making tech companies cover their data centers’ electricity price impacts. The New Mexico Democrat blocked the Ohio Republican’s effort to pass the Ratepayer Protection Act through unanimous consent, arguing that the bill…
articles.body:
Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) blocked Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Thursday effort to unanimously pass a bill that seeks to force states to consider making tech companies cover their data centers’ electricity price impacts.

The New Mexico Democrat blocked the Ohio Republican’s effort to pass the Ratepayer Protection Act through unanimous consent, arguing that the bill is toothless.

The bill, which passed the House 417-3 on Wednesday, forces states to hold a hearing on rules to make data centers pay for increased electricity costs from their operations, but it does not make states adopt any such standards or force tech companies to cover the costs.

“It’s not enough for us to tell states to consider making data centers pay for grid updates. Rather than voluntary pledges or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth,” Heinrich said.

Husted, ahead of Heinrich’s objection, said the bill “would require state utility regulators to consider standards ensuring that large load customers pay the full incremental cost of the infrastructure needed to serve them.”

“This is how we make sure American families are not left footing the bill for energy infrastructure required by data centers,” Husted added.

After he objected to the unanimous passage of Husted’s bill, Heinrich attempted to unanimously pass his Grid Savings Act , which he said would “require large load customers like data centers to pay for the facilities needed to connect them to the grid, not to consider it, not to make pledges, to actually do it, to pay for the upgrades they need.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) objected to Heinrich’s push.

“The term ‘do-nothing Congress’ exists for a reason. We absolutely accomplished that right now. We did nothing here in the Senate because, again, of Democrat obstruction. This bill would have done something that’s not nothing,” Moreno said.

“The victim of all this is the taxpayer of the United States of America, who’s going to see electricity prices continue to go up because we could have passed a law to solve it. Instead, it’s more games after more games. Like the American people, I’m sick of it, and I know they are. And for that reason, I object,” he added.

Husted, meanwhile, pointed out that his bill had adequate support in the House and was on track to become law.

“The reason that I’m proposing that we pass this piece of legislation is because it passed the House 417-3. If the gentleman from New Mexico’s provision had passed the House 417-3, he would have every right to stand up and ask that we do this. But before we leave here, we ought to do something on a matter that the American people have asked us to do something about, and we have the opportunity to do that with the Ratepayer Protection Act,” he said.

“It is a shame that this opportunity has been missed today, but I will be back to push this issue forward. We have a bipartisan opportunity to get this done, we should do it immediately,” he added.

articles.title: Haaland backs data center moratorium in New Mexico
articles.summary: New Mexico gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland (D) on Thursday backed a moratorium on the construction of data centers in her state, citing environmental and workforce-related concerns. In a policy framework on her website, Haaland backed “open, transparent, and meaningful” conversations within communities about the impacts of AI data centers. She also called for requiring data…
articles.body:
New Mexico gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland (D) on Thursday backed a moratorium on the construction of data centers in her state, citing environmental and workforce-related concerns.

In a policy framework on her website, Haaland backed “open, transparent, and meaningful” conversations within communities about the impacts of AI data centers.

She also called for requiring data centers to build their own renewable energy infrastructure to prevent energy costs from trickling down to New Mexicans and establishing safeguards to protect the environment. Data centers must be “built and run with New Mexico labor,” Haaland’s proposal noted.

Haaland, the Biden administration’s Interior secretary, said in a statement that New Mexicans “are right to be concerned” about the rapid development of data centers.

“Our communities should be protected. That’s why I support a moratorium on data centers until the state adopts clear and transparent accountability measures for this industry,” added Haaland, who is running against Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho.

The former Interior secretary and congresswoman also argued her state “has the opportunity to lead the way” on how to protect our communities, safeguard our water, boost our economy, and sustain our environment for generations to come.”

The Hill has reached out to Hull’s campaign for comment.

There are 21 operational data centers in New Mexico, with one such facility under construction, five planned, one paused and one inactive, according to the U.S. Data Center Map .

The risk to the state’s climate, as assessed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, from data centers is relatively high, per the tracking project.

A growing number of Americans and politicians have called for curbs on data center construction. That comes as concerns on Capitol Hill percolate about rapidly advancing AI models .

Data centers accounted for more than 4 percent of the country’s electricity consumption in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA) and Pew Research Center . The IEA projected last year that U.S. data centers’ electricity consumption will increase by nearly 133 percent by 2030.

articles.title: Crypto shifts focus to Trump regulators after coming up short in Senate
articles.summary: A cryptocurrency regulation bill appears to have little momentum left in the Senate after it came up short in a floor vote Tuesday, with the industry now turning its attention to Trump administration regulators to set the rules of the road. The Clarity Act failed to secure enough support to clear a procedural hurdle Tuesday…
articles.body:
A cryptocurrency regulation bill appears to have little momentum left in the Senate after it came up short in a floor vote Tuesday, with the industry now turning its attention to Trump administration regulators to set the rules of the road.

The Clarity Act failed to secure enough support to clear a procedural hurdle Tuesday afternoon, with every Democrat and several Republicans voting against the effort to advance the bill.

It was a stinging loss for an industry that has poured extensive resources into lobbying Congress for the legislation over the past two years, as well as the GOP lawmakers and administration officials who championed the push.

But crypto leaders are quickly shifting their hopes to a pair of financial regulators in the Trump administration: the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

“The Senate has voted and we have a different type of clarity. It’s time for agencies to step forward and for crypto voters to make their voice heard,” Faryar Shirzad, Coinbase’s chief policy officer, wrote in a post Tuesday on the social platform X.

Support for the Clarity Act crumbled after crypto-friendly Democrats and Republicans failed to reach an agreement on ethics language ahead of Tuesday’s vote.

Ethics were a longtime concern for Democrats, who voiced worries about passing legislation that could potentially boost President Trump and his family’s crypto businesses.

Senate Republicans put forward what an aide described as their “last, best and final offer” on Sunday with a new White House-backed ethics provision.

But Democrats indicated Monday the updated language still fell short, with Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) telling reporters there were “a whole lot of loopholes.”

Talks continued up until Tuesday’s vote, in which Democrats ultimately blocked the legislation. They were joined by four Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Josh Hawley (Mo.), Jerry Moran (Kan.) and Thom Tillis (N.C.).

Both sides traded blame after the measure came up short. Democrats accused Republican leaders of cutting negotiations short and failing to stand up to Trump.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) argued Tuesday that his GOP counterparts spent time “twisting themselves into knots to appease” the president rather than working with Democrats to “craft a bill that could pass with strong ethics provisions.”

Republicans tossed the onus back on their colleagues across the aisle, accusing them of continuously moving the goal posts. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) suggested the vote showed that Democrats “were never truly serious” about the effort.

“I sat at the table with Senate Democrats working in good faith to get this done while they played games,” she said in a statement.

Several senators have attempted to leave the door open to future talks.

Tillis, who switched his vote to “no” at the last minute and put forward a motion to reconsider the bill, underscored Tuesday that the move “allows us to continue working towards a positive outcome,” declaring this is “not the end for the Clarity Act.”

A group of seven Democrats — Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), Cory Booker (N.J.), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Mark Warner (Va.), Gallego and Warnock — similarly argued Wednesday that they were still committed to getting the bill across the finish line.

“Democrats have spent the last two years working to pass crypto legislation that would expand opportunity, protect consumers, punish bad actors, create regulatory certainty, and include strong, commonsense ethics provisions for elected officials,” they said in a statement.

“This week was a setback, but not the end of that important work,” they continued. “We remain committed to working in a bipartisan fashion to get this legislation passed.”

But many in Congress and the industry viewed the failed vote as the end of the line for the Clarity Act this year. One Senate GOP aide told The Hill on Tuesday that their boss “thinks it is dead.”

In a signal of where momentum is headed, Patrick Witt, the president’s chief crypto adviser, pointed to the chairs of the SEC and the CFTC on Tuesday, saying “you’re up.”

The two financial regulators were always expected to oversee the crypto market. The Clarity Act chiefly sought to figure out how to split responsibilities between the SEC and the CFTC, drawing a line between when digital assets are securities and commodities.

While the industry preferred the more permanent nature of legislation, both agencies have been making moves to tee up their own regulations.

“We think the SEC and CFTC will shift into overdrive with aggressive, pro-industry proposals,” Ian Katz, managing director at Capital Alpha, wrote in a note Tuesday. “The Republican leadership at those agencies will be able to pass regulations without Democratic approval.”

“Some of those proposals may come with an implied message to Democrats amounting to: This is what you get when you don’t legislate,” he continued.

CFTC Chair Michael Selig vowed Wednesday to “get the job done using our existing statutory authorities,” adding in a post on X that the agency is “locked in and ready to ship its rules for the new frontier of finance.”

SEC Chair Paul Atkins similarly hinted Wednesday at upcoming action from the agency. On Thursday, the commission announced its long-awaited “innovation exemption.”

The order helps clear the way for tokenized stock trading by exempting platforms and liquidity providers from traditional securities rules.

“Earlier this week, Congress was unsuccessful in advancing the CLARITY Act despite the tireless efforts of many,” Atkins said in a statement Thursday.

“So today, the Securities and Exchange Commission is taking a significant step forward, within its statutory authority, to bring America’s capital markets into the digital age by facilitating onchain trading of certain tokenized stocks through the ‘Innovation Exemption.’”

It marks the latest in a series of efforts by the Trump regulators to bring rules to the crypto market, even as lawmakers attempt to hash out legislation.

The SEC previously put forward rulemaking in August to create a pair of new exemptions, allowing issuers to offer crypto assets without needing to register first with the commission.

The agency also clarified what types of digital assets fall under its purview earlier this year, noting that digital or tokenized securities are largely the only crypto assets within its domain. The CFTC said it would administer commodities law consistent with this view.

As the two regulators charge ahead, the prospect that Congress revives the Clarity Act later this year are “dim,” Katz noted.

The House is out of session up until after the midterms, and there are only about five more weeks in 2026 when both chambers are in session, leaving little time to maneuver.

While the measure could be reintroduced next year in the new Congress, “much of the bill would have to be reworked,” Katz added. Democrats are widely expected to take control of the House, with Senate control still up in the air.

“Lawmakers wouldn’t quite be starting from scratch, but it would probably feel like that to the bill’s proponents,” he said. “It’s also possible that Democratic demands would be so unpleasant for the crypto industry that it might prefer no bill at all.”

articles.title: Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency assistance amid RFK Jr. clash over measles
articles.summary: Pennsylvania’s health department has started the process of requesting emergency assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to help control a deadly and rapidly spreading measles outbreak, according to a letter sent to the CDC from state officials. But the request for that assistance, known as Epi-Aid, comes on the condition that…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania’s health department has started the process of requesting emergency assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to help control a deadly and rapidly spreading measles outbreak, according to a letter sent to the CDC from state officials.

But the request for that assistance, known as Epi-Aid, comes on the condition that the CDC publicly recognize the four people in the commonwealth who have died from measles-related complications, which the agency has so far refused to do.

In the letter, Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen said it was important for state and federal officials to have a trusting relationship based on “respectful, transparent, and factual communication.”

“The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the Department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.”

The Keystone State’s measles outbreak has been the focal point of an ongoing bitter political dispute between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) — a potential 2028 presidential candidate — and Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Kennedy has openly questioned whether the deaths in Pennsylvania were directly caused by measles and accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak. The CDC in turn has been excluding the deaths from its weekly national measles death tally, a radical departure from the typical agency practice of accepting a state’s own reporting.

Pennsylvania to date has declined offers of federal assistance because they have been handling the outbreak internally, though Bogen in the letter noted the health department has been meeting regularly with CDC staff and recently made two requests for technical assistance.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for HHS, said in a statement the CDC has not received the formal Epi-Aid request “through its normal channels.”

“CDC will not submit to political blackmail that conditions critical public health assistance. The people of Pennsylvania should never be used as leverage in a political dispute over how deaths are classified,” Hilliard said.

“CDC will not allow Governor Shapiro to politicize this process. We owe the American people accurate, consistent, and transparent public health information,” she added.

The agency typically relies on state health officials to investigate and report measles cases to the federal government. Public health experts and former agency officials have said it’s highly unusual for the CDC to dispute how a state classifies and reports measles cases and deaths, and the situation could undermine how states interact with the federal government in the future.

The CDC said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized definition for a measles death “to ensure consistent reporting across jurisdictions.”

Any deaths will only be counted if the agency’s National Center for Health Statistics identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states.

On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania health department announced that 731 measles cases have been confirmed in 38 counties across the state so far this year. Four people have died in the state from measles-related illness as of Tuesday.

articles.title: F-16 crashes on training run in Michigan; pilot safely ejects
articles.summary: An F-16 fighter jet crashed and the pilot ejected to safety in northern Michigan on Thursday afternoon, military officials confirmed. The crash, which occurred in Grand Traverse County, was captured in a video circulated by local news outlets showing a large plume of black smoke in the air near residential homes. The Texas Military Department…
articles.body:
An F-16 fighter jet crashed and the pilot ejected to safety in northern Michigan on Thursday afternoon, military officials confirmed.

The crash, which occurred in Grand Traverse County, was captured in a video circulated by local news outlets showing a large plume of black smoke in the air near residential homes.

The Texas Military Department said the F-16 belonged to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing and was on a routine training mission from the Air National Guard’s Combat Readiness Training Center in Alpena when it crashed.

“The pilot successfully ejected the aircraft and is receiving care at a nearby hospital,” the department said in a statement. “Emergency responders are on-site. The incident is under investigation.”

Michigan State Police ordered people within a mile of the crash site to evacuate due to a hazardous chemical spill linked to the aircraft. Residents had earlier been told to shelter in place and close their windows and doors.

The cause of the crash has not been determined. Air traffic control audio , however, suggests a possible bird strike occurred shortly before the F-16 went down.

Military officials have not confirmed that the aircraft struck a bird.

The 149th Fighter Wing, known as the Lone Star Gunfighters, is an F-16 unit based at Joint Base San-Antonio Lackland in Texas. The unit had sent student and instructor pilots to Michigan for Operation Northern Cactus, a training exercise at the Alpena center.
